session.title: How should urgency feel?
session.intro: Relay has to make ownership unmistakable without making every incident feel catastrophic. Compare the hierarchy, language, and interaction—not just the color.

context.product_job: Help the next on-call engineer understand what changed, who owns the response, and what must happen now.
context.audience: Engineers receiving a live production incident, often tired, interrupted, and scanning under time pressure.
context.primary_action: Acknowledge the incident and take ownership.
constraints: Existing React application with a compact desktop shell
Must remain legible at 200% zoom and in high-contrast mode
Real incident titles and ownership language—no placeholder metrics

questions.prompt: Which hierarchy makes a live handoff feel decisive without becoming an alarm dashboard?
questions.help: Each specimen uses the same incident and action. Choose the reading order you trust when attention is fragmented.

options.label: Command brief
options.thesis: A sharp editorial headline states the changed condition; restrained interface type carries the operational detail.
options.fit: It gives the incident one memorable sentence before exposing the work, which helps a receiving engineer orient quickly.
options.change: Incident state becomes the dominant line; ownership and elapsed time move into a quiet evidence row.
options.risk: Large editorial type can feel theatrical if routine warnings receive the same treatment as an outage.
options.cost: Moderate—new type roles and responsive hierarchy, familiar controls.

specimen.title: Retries are exhausting the write queue.
specimen.body: Morgan handed off after isolating the regression to the eu-west workers. No customer data has been lost.
specimen.annotation: The incident sentence leads; severity supports it instead of becoming the whole personality.

options.label: Operations ledger
options.thesis: A compact, evidence-first surface lets timestamps, ownership, and system state establish trust before the action.
options.fit: It matches how experienced responders read an incident: scan the facts, verify scope, then accept responsibility.
options.change: The product becomes denser and more procedural, with a stable two-column fact rhythm and quieter titles.
options.risk: It may make new responders work too hard to understand which fact matters most.
options.cost: Low—mostly type, spacing, and information-order changes.

specimen.title: Write queue retry exhaustion
specimen.body: Scope confirmed in eu-west. Handoff notes and runbook checks are complete.
specimen.annotation: The timeline is the interface spine; the action remains visually singular.

options.label: Calm relay
options.thesis: A human, measured interface treats handoff as a clear transfer between people rather than a machine shouting at both of them.
options.fit: It can lower panic while keeping accountability explicit, especially for incidents that last across shifts.
options.change: Ownership language and the next safe action lead; severity is confined to one strong signal line.
options.risk: The softer tone could understate rare, truly catastrophic incidents unless severity escalation is proven separately.
options.cost: Moderate—copy, state semantics, and escalation treatment need joint design.

specimen.title: Morgan has prepared the next move.
specimen.body: The retry source is isolated. Take ownership, then verify the queue after the worker restart.
specimen.annotation: Person-to-person language carries the transition; urgency stays in the evidence.

questions.prompt: What should the ownership transfer communicate at the decisive moment?
questions.help: This choice governs copy, motion, confirmation, and what remains visible after the handoff—not a decorative animation preference.

options.label: Signed transfer
options.thesis: Treat acceptance like a signed operational event with a clear before, after, and durable timestamp.
options.fit: Accountability is the product job, so the interaction should leave no ambiguity about who owns the next action.
options.change: The control becomes a two-step confirmation only when the incident is P1; the resulting ownership record stays in view.
options.risk: Extra confirmation becomes friction if applied to routine incidents.

specimen.title: You will own Incident 2841.
specimen.body: Morgan remains attached for ten minutes. Your first verification is due at 19:03.
specimen.annotation: One consequential confirmation; the completed state becomes evidence, not confetti.

options.label: Continuous relay
options.thesis: Make transfer immediate, then keep the previous owner and next check visible so continuity matters more than ceremony.
options.fit: Long incidents are collaborative; this avoids pretending responsibility changes in a single clean instant.
options.change: Acceptance is one action, followed by a persistent handoff strip with both people and the next verification.
options.risk: Immediate acceptance needs a strong undo or correction path for accidental taps.
options.cost: Low to moderate—persistent state and a bounded correction path.

specimen.title: You have the incident. Morgan is still here.
specimen.body: Verify the queue at 19:03. Correct the owner from the timeline if this transfer was accidental.
specimen.annotation: The completion state preserves continuity and gives the next action a real home.
